A1-A2.headline: The Long History of People Who Trade Goods

pages.text: Imagine a world without stores. How would you get your food or clothes? Merchants are people who buy and sell things to help us get what we need. They work in shops or online. Merchants have been part of human life for thousands of years, helping build trade in many old countries.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text: The Phoenicians were very famous traders. They lived near the sea a long time ago. They sold things like purple dye, glass, and wine. They also helped spread their alphabet to other people. This made it easier for many people to write and trade.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text: In ancient Rome, being a merchant was not always seen as a good job. Some people thought farming was better. But some merchants became very rich. They sold fish sauce and other goods to people far away. They even traveled to China for trade.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a garum container from Pompeii

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text: The word merchant comes from an old Latin word for trading. Artists in the 1500s liked to paint merchants. These paintings show us how they lived and worked. Merchants were important for the growth of towns and cities all over the world.

evidence.articleCaption: Costumes of merchants from Brabant and Antwerp, engraving by Abraham de Bruyn, 1577

B1-B2.headline: From Ancient Markets to Global Trade Networks

pages.text: Picture a bustling ancient bazaar filled with exotic scents and goods. Merchants are the people who connect producers to buyers, whether through local shops or global trade. This profession has existed as long as human commerce itself. From ancient times to modern online platforms, merchants have been the essential link driving economic growth.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text: The Phoenicians were among the most influential traders in history. By the 9th century BCE, they dominated Mediterranean trade. They exported goods like wood, cloth, and their famous purple dye. They also spread their efficient alphabet, which simplified record-keeping and communication for other cultures throughout the region.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text: Social status for merchants varied greatly. In Rome, trade was often viewed as less respectable than farming, yet some merchants achieved great wealth. For instance, Umbricius Scaurus became famous for his high-quality fish sauce. Roman trade networks were vast, with evidence showing that Roman goods reached as far as southern China by 226 CE.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a Roman fish sauce jar

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text: The term merchant originates from the Latin word for trading. By the 16th century, artists began to focus on merchants as subjects for their work. These portraits and group paintings documented the rise of powerful mercantile organizations, reflecting the growing influence of the merchant class in European society and their role in shaping modern economies.

C1-C2.headline: The Enduring Legacy of the Mercantile Class

pages.text: Merchants serve as the fundamental conduits of global commerce, facilitating the exchange of goods through physical storefronts and digital marketplaces. Their historical trajectory spans from the dawn of civilization to the present day, consistently acting as catalysts for economic expansion. By integrating financial and intellectual capital, they have historically bridged the gap between disparate markets and cultures.
pages.caption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck

evidence.fileTitle: File:Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c1660.jpg
evidence.articleCaption: Merchants in a Southern Port by Thomas Wyck c. 1660

pages.text: The Phoenicians established a formidable maritime hegemony, utilizing their monopoly on purple dye to dominate Mediterranean trade routes. Beyond the exchange of tangible commodities like glass and textiles, they were instrumental in the dissemination of their phonetic alphabet. This innovation revolutionized administrative efficiency, enabling complex correspondence across their expansive network of colonies and trading outposts.
pages.caption: Phoenician traders across the Mediterranean region

imageProvenance.imageAttribution: Publisher New York Ward, Lock (Public domain)

evidence.articleCaption: Phoenician merchants traded across the entire Mediterranean region

pages.text: The social standing of merchants was historically contingent upon cultural perceptions; while Middle Eastern bazaars elevated them to local elites, Roman society often relegated them to lower status despite their potential for significant wealth. Figures like Umbricius Scaurus exemplified this dichotomy, amassing vast fortunes through specialized production. Their reach was truly global, with archaeological evidence confirming long-distance trade with China.
pages.caption: Mosaic showing a garum container from Pompeii

evidence.articleCaption: Mosaic showing garum container, from the house of Umbricius Scaurus of Pompeii. The inscription which reads "G(ari) F(los) SCO(mbri) SCAURI EX OFFI(CI)NA SCAURI" has been translated as "The flower of garum, made of the mackerel, a product of Scaurus, from the shop of Scaurus"

pages.text: Etymologically rooted in the Latin 'mercatare', the term merchant has evolved alongside the profession itself. During the 16th century, the merchant class became a focal point for artistic representation, with painters documenting the rise of influential guilds. These artworks serve as historical evidence of the merchant's transition from mere trader to a central architect of modern economic development.
